content_voiceover: This table is a high-yield summary for the differential diagnosis of an abdominal mass in a child. Wilms tumor peaks between two and five years old, arises in the kidney, and spreads to lung and liver. Hepatoblastoma peaks under two years old, arises in the liver, and spreads to the lungs. Desmoplastic small round cell tumor, or DSRCT, is different, it hits older kids and adolescents and young adults, can arise anywhere in the abdomen, and spreads along the peritoneum. Neuroblastoma peaks under five years old, arises from the adrenal gland or sympathetic chain, and spreads to bone marrow, liver, and skin. Rhabdomyosarcoma can occur at any age, arising from the prostate, uterus, bladder, or biliary tract, and spreads to lung, bone marrow, and lymph nodes. Ewing sarcoma, also any age, classically arises in the pelvis and spreads to lung and bone marrow. Lymphoma can arise anywhere in the abdomen at any age, spreading to bone marrow, skin, and CSF. And germ cell tumors, especially in adolescence, arise in the ovary, sacrum, or coccyx, spreading to lung, liver, and occasionally bone.
keypoints: Wilms tumor, kidney, peak age two to five, spreads to lung and liver
Hepatoblastoma, liver, peak under two, spreads to lungs
Neuroblastoma, adrenal or sympathetic chain, peak under five, spreads to bone marrow and liver
DSRCT and lymphoma can occur anywhere in the abdomen at any age
keypoint_voiceover: When you see an abdominal mass, let age and location narrow things down fast. Under five, think Wilms if it is kidney-based, neuroblastoma if it is adrenal or paraspinal, and hepatoblastoma if it is liver-based. In older children and adolescents, broaden your differential to rhabdomyosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma, lymphoma, DSRCT, and germ cell tumors, since those can show up at any age.
